to hunt sleeping bushbabies.
By the end, Doug stands where one chimp family split in two,
and one half started killing the other.
Distant relatives.
The Spear.

shots.narration: and sometimes chew the tip into a point.

elements.text: SPLIT: MORE THAN 60 MILLION YEARS AGO

shots.narration: and they carry it straight to a hollow tree.

elements.text: SPLIT: MORE THAN 60 MILLION YEARS AGO

shots.narration: They jab it into the hole again and again,

elements.text: SPLIT: MORE THAN 60 MILLION YEARS AGO

shots.narration: because a lesser bushbaby spends the day asleep inside hollows exactly like this one.

shots.narration: Apart from people, these chimpanzees are the only animals known to regularly hunt animals with backbones using tools.

elements.text: SPLIT: MORE THAN 60 MILLION YEARS AGO

shots.narration: The Monkey Hunt.
At Ngogo, in Uganda, the chimpanzees ate so many red colobus monkeys
that the local population of those monkeys fell by almost nine tenths.
Red colobus are true monkeys, and their family line split from the apes about twenty-five to thirty million years ago.
Chimpanzees are not monkeys, and they are the ones doing the hunting.
The chimpanzee community at Ngogo is the largest ever recorded,
and most of its kills are made by adult males hunting in groups.
The colobus do fight back, and when chimps attack, the adult colobus males gather to defend the group,
and bigger groups have more defenders, which makes them harder to hunt.
The problem is the arithmetic.
Over about thirty-three years of counts, the red colobus population at Ngogo fell by an estimated eighty-nine percent,
and the researchers concluded that chimpanzee hunting was the main cause.
That's like a town of a thousand people shrinking to about a hundred and ten.
It may be the first recorded case of an animal other than us driving down another primate's numbers.
Doug, dressed as a red colobus, has found the safest spot in the forest,
directly behind three very large colobus males.
The chimps pick a different tree.
Doug is fine.
The defence works on the day, but at Ngogo, over the years, it didn't.
Monkeys are cousins at about thirty million years,
and the next relative on the tree is an ape.
Close relatives.
The Gorilla.
In twenty nineteen, in Gabon, researchers watched chimpanzees kill gorillas,
the first lethal attacks of chimps on gorillas ever recorded.
Until then, the two apes had mostly got along.
In Loango National Park, scientists saw nine meetings between twenty fourteen and twenty eighteen,
every one of them peaceful, and twice the two species fed in the same fruit trees.
Then, twice in twenty nineteen, a party of twenty-seven chimpanzees ran into a gorilla group,
first a group of five and later a group of seven.
Twenty-seven chimps is a whole school class.
The gorillas fought back, and in the first meeting the silverback charged
and knocked a young chimp into the air.
Then about nine males surrounded him, and he backed away with his group.
The disturbing part is which gorilla they went for.
Size didn't decide the fight. Numbers did.
Both times, the gorilla that died was one of the smallest in its group.
The researchers suggest it may be competition,
because both attacks came in months when fruit was scarce,
and chimps, gorillas and forest elephants all want the same trees.
Doug, in a dark gorilla suit, sits proudly between two silverbacks.
Chimps appear on the ridge: ten, twenty, twenty-seven,
and the silverbacks stand up.
Doug is the smallest gorilla here.
Doug has died,
in a gorilla suit.
Gorillas split from chimps about eight to ten million years ago,
and the next relative to branch off wears a red cap.
The Human.
Chimpanzees are more closely related to humans than they are to gorillas.
Humans and chimps share an ancestor that lived about six to seven million years ago.
Gorillas branched off before that, so a gorilla is as distant from a chimp as it is from us.
Line up the two genomes, and where single letters can be compared,
about ninety-nine in every hundred are the same.
It's like two copies of a long novel with roughly one letter in every hundred changed,
and that count leaves out bigger chunks that were added or lost.
Wild chimpanzees sometimes attack people, mostly where farms meet the forest.
At Bossou, in Guinea, researchers recorded eleven attacks on local people between nineteen ninety-five and two thousand nine,
and none of them was fatal.
They happened on roads, paths and fields beside the forest,
in seasons when wild fruit was scarce and the chimps were raiding crops like maize.
Here's the uncomfortable part.
The gorilla Doug was dressed as a minute ago is a more distant cousin to the chimp than Doug himself is.
He doesn't need a costume, because he's already the relative.
Doug has already lost an arm-wrestle to one of these,
and today he walks a farm track at the forest edge with a sack of maize,
waving at the trees.
Doug has died,
even though none of the Bossou attacks was fatal.
Doug has always been an overachiever.
Gorillas are further from chimps than we are,
but one ape is closer than us, and it lives across a river.
The Bonobo.
The chimpanzee's closest living relative almost never kills anyone.
Bonobos and chimpanzees split about one to two million years ago,
and today bonobos live only south of the Congo River, while chimps live north and east of it.
The river probably split them.
The Congo is the deepest river ever measured, at about two hundred and twenty meters in places.
Stand two football pitches on end, one on top of the other,
and the top one would still be underwater.
That's not even the strange part.
Scientists pooled five decades of records from eighteen chimp communities and four bonobo communities,
and the bonobo total was one suspected killing.
Doug is wearing the chimp costume with a hand-written name tag that says bonobo,
and he's sitting in a bonobo group south of the river.
Nothing happens. Doug is fine.
The closest relative is the safe one, and only because there's a river in the way.
Now cross the river, because on the other side the relatives are the same species.
Same species.
The Patrol.
Chimpanzees are loud almost all the time,
except when they are going looking for trouble.
At Ngogo, a group of males will get up without warning, form a single line
and walk off in silence toward the edge of their territory.
A normal chimp party is loud and spread out, and a patrol is quiet and tight.
In the first detailed study there, a patrol went out about once every ten days,
with an average of thirteen chimps, almost all of them males.
That's a football team, plus two on the bench.
Ngogo has so many males that it patrols about twice as often as other well-studied communities.
A patrol takes about two hours,
and on most of them they meet nobody, or only hear the neighbours far away.
But if they find a stranger and they outnumber it, they attack.
The worst part is the quiet.
Doug is still dressed as a chimp, because dressing as the hunter seemed like the safe option.
He's walking alone along a ridge on the wrong side of the river, whistling.
The forest goes quiet first.
Then Doug does.
Doug has died, quietly.
One stranger is a patrol, but a whole neighbouring family is a project.
The Neighbours.
Between nineteen ninety-eight and two thousand eight, the Ngogo chimpanzees killed twenty-one chimps from neighbouring groups.
Thirteen of them lived in one area to the northeast,
and in two thousand nine, Ngogo moved in.
The territory grew by about six point four square kilometers, a twenty-two percent increase,
or nearly nine hundred football pitches of forest.
Here's what makes it disturbing. It paid off.
In the three years before the expansion, Ngogo's females had fifteen babies,
and in the three years after it, they had thirty-seven.
The chance of a baby dying before age three fell from forty-one percent to eight,
and the study suggests the new land meant better-fed mothers.
The fruit back home had not improved, so the extra food came from the land they took.
It wasn't random violence. It was real estate.
Doug has moved into the northeast in his chimp costume,
built himself a tidy nest and put up a sign with his name on it.
The sign comes down first.
The territory has a new owner,
and Doug has died.
That was strangers, and the next one is a chimp who used to be in charge.
Family.
The Old King.
In twenty thirteen, a chimpanzee who used to rule Fongoli was killed by members of his own community.
This is the spear community from the start,
and his name was Foudouko.
He had been the alpha male, so dominant that the others feared him,
and after he lost that place, he was exiled.
He spent about five years on the outskirts,
following the group from a distance and meeting old allies in private,
which is longer than most people keep a phone.
When he came back in twenty thirteen, nobody saw what happened next.
That's what makes this one unusual.
Most chimp violence is between communities,
and killing a member of your own is extremely rare,
and nobody had ever recorded an exile this long.
Here's the catch. Fongoli has more males than females,
so the competition for mates is fierce,
and the younger males may have feared he would take power again.
Doug, still in his chimp costume, thinks someone should welcome the old king home,
so he has made him a paper crown.
The group notices the crown.
Doug has died,
and the crown was a mistake.
Foudouko was one chimp who came back,
but in the last one, a whole family splits in two.
The Split.
The largest chimpanzee community ever known has split in two,
and since twenty eighteen, one half has been killing the other.
Ngogo had about two hundred members,
and in twenty fifteen two clusters started avoiding each other,
and by twenty eighteen they were separate groups with separate land.
It's like a school year of two hundred kids drawing a line down the playground,
and the line never coming back up.
Between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-four, the Western group killed seven adult males from the Central group,
and seventeen of the smallest.
Some of those chimps had been on friendly terms for years.
Genetic evidence suggests splits like this happen about once every five hundred years,
and the only other case on record was at Gombe, in Tanzania, in the nineteen seventies.
The breakaway males were killed or vanished one by one,
in what primatologists call the Four-Year War.
The worst part is who they kill.
A chimp's closest relative is the one it grew up with,
and here, that's the one it kills.
Chimpanzees are listed as Endangered, mostly because of hunting, lost forest and disease.
Doug wants to stay friends with everyone, so he's standing exactly on the line.
Both sides look at him.
Each has decided he belongs to the other one.
The family tree doesn't protect anyone,
it just tells you who's next.
Doug deaths: three hundred and eight.
Doug's next mistake is on your screen now.
The cap stays on the line.
Nobody crosses for it, because it belongs to both sides.
